query: Consider the following context: The recent perspective of multiprincipal element alloys (MPEAs), also known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs), has emerged as a very promising area for material design. Additive manufacturing (AM) strategies have also been noted to provide additional strength to HEA systems. In the selected dual-nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA system, an additional strength of approximately 300–400 MPa was achieved by adopting an additive manufacturing route as compared to its cast and wrought counterparts. However, the challenge of oxidation degradation always imposes a severe limitation for high-temperature applications in gas turbines, power plants, and aerospace components. Hence, ensuring material sustainability, longevity, and integrity for high-temperature applications inevitably requires the exploration of the oxidation behavior of alloys. In that context, which method can be used for elucidating the mechanistic aspects and elemental redistribution of nanoprecipitates on oxidation behavior, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Applying atom probe tomography (APT) to oxidized dual‐nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA samples will reveal that high-temperature oxidation induces a nanoscale redistribution of elements within and around the nanoprecipitates, contributing to the formation of protective oxide phases.
generation.material_initial_state: Dual-nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy produced via additive manufacturing, exhibiting uniformly distributed nanoprecipitates in the matrix.
generation.intervention: Exposure to high-temperature oxidative conditions (simulated service temperatures relevant to gas turbine, power plant, or aerospace applications).
generation.conditions: Isothermal oxidation treatments in air (or controlled oxygen atmosphere) at temperatures typical for high-temperature applications, for set durations designed to promote elemental diffusion and oxide scale formation.
generation.structural_mediator: The nanoscale distribution and interfaces of the nanoprecipitates within the HEA matrix.
generation.mechanism: High-temperature oxidation leads to selective elemental migration, where oxidation‐resistant species (e.g., Al, Cr, or Ti) are enriched at nanoprecipitate/matrix interfaces, facilitating the development of a protective oxide scale while possibly altering the internal precipitate composition.
generation.predicted_outcome: APT will detect compositional gradients at and around the nanoprecipitates, indicating an elemental redistribution that correlates with enhanced oxidation resistance. Compared to the as-manufactured (non-oxidized) state, oxidized samples are expected to show a localized enrichment of certain oxidation-resistant elements.
generation.baseline: Elemental distribution characterized in the unoxidized, additive-manufactured state of the HEA.
generation.boundary: This phenomenon is hypothesized under controlled oxidation conditions; deviations in temperature, oxygen partial pressure, or exposure time may lead to different redistribution dynamics or introduce additional phases not captured in this test.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitudes of the elemental shifts and the spatial extent of the gradients are uncertain, as are potential contributions from minor phases or effects due to specimen preparation for APT.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare HEA samples in the as-manufactured state and subject them to controlled high-temperature oxidation treatments. Use APT to map the three-dimensional elemental distributions across and near the nanoprecipitates in both the oxidized and unoxidized samples.
measurements: 3D compositional maps detailing elemental gradients at nanoprecipitate boundaries.
Quantitative analysis of the enrichment (or depletion) of oxidation-resistant elements (e.g., Al, Cr, Ti) at the interfaces.
Comparison of the spatial distribution profiles between oxidized and baseline samples.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If APT analysis fails to reveal significant differences in elemental distribution or gradients at the nanoprecipitate interfaces between oxidized and unoxidized samples, or if no correlation is found between such redistribution and the formation of protective oxide phases, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Question: How can the compressive strength of the NbMoCrTiAl refractory high-entropy alloy be improved for high-temperature structural applications while maintaining oxidation resistance?. System: NbMoCrTiAl high entropy alloy matrix with in-situ formed TiC and Al2O3 reinforcement particles. Processing: High energy planetary ball milling for 39 h at 300 rpm with stearic acid as process control agent, followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1700 °C under 30 MPa axial pressure for 30 min. Test conditions: Room temperature compression tests at a strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1 on cylindrical specimens (4 mm diameter, 6 mm height).
